item.title: Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches drones at Russia
item.description: Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches drones at Russia

Blaze at St Petersburg oil sites as Kyiv launches drones at Russia The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure

Plumes of smoke rise from fires (centre) at an oil refinery following what the authorities say is a Ukrainian drone strike in the course of the Russia-Ukraine conflict | REUTERS

AP Moscow 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 4:03 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Ukrainian attacks set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg on Sunday, as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments. The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington, with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov. A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea. Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said. Also Read

How geopolitical stigma associated with Putin is affecting Russians

Many don't know what my decision is: Trump on Russia sanctions waiver

Zelenskyy criticizes Trump's waiver of sanctions on Russia as 'wrong'

Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said. Russia continues energy attacks, Kyiv says US President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.

Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus. Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the ceasefire. In a post on X Sunday, Zelenskyy said that in the week since Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia had attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times. He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.

"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote. Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia's invasion - not because Ukraine was defending itself. "It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.

(Only the headline and picture of this report may have been reworked by the Business Standard staff; the rest of the content is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

item.title: Highways ministry invokes catastrophic failure clause against 2 developers
item.description: The Highways Ministry has invoked the newly introduced provision of the catastrophic failure clause against two highway developers for major structural failures on National Highways projects.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Industry / News / Highways ministry invokes catastrophic failure clause against 2 developers

Highways ministry invokes catastrophic failure clause against 2 developers The project was sanctioned for Rs 2,061 crore, and EPC work was awarded to the joint venture of VRC Constructions (India) Pvt Ltd and R & C Infra Engineers Pvt Ltd at a contract price of Rs 613 crore

Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 3:41 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The Highways Ministry has invoked the newly introduced provision of the catastrophic failure clause against two highway developers for major structural failures on National Highways projects. The provisions of the catastrophic event allow highway-owning agencies to bar highway developers for two years from bidding for new projects. Such highway builders also face negative ratings that will adversely impact their chances of getting future projects. According to documents accessed by PTI, the Road Transport and Highways Ministry has notified a catastrophic event in a project comprising the four-lane Poondiankuppam-Sattanatharupam section of NH-45 (New NH-32) from km 67 to km 123 in Tamil Nadu under HAM mode.   "The bid project cost was Rs 2,120 crore, and it was awarded to M/S Poonadinkuppam Sattanathapuram Section Private Limited (Promoters-M/s Oriental) under a concession agreement. The appointed date of the project was January 20, 2022, with a scheduled completion date of January 19, 2024. "M/s Theme Engineering Services Private Limited has been appointed as the independent engineer," the ministry's order said. Also Read

The order document further said that at approximately 0030 hours on April 6, 2026, substantial settlement of the pavement quality concrete of approximately 2 metres was observed on the main carriageway at the approach to the light vehicle underpass at km 105+220 on the Kollidam Bypass. The incident was accompanied by bulging, cracking and horizontal displacement of the reinforced earth. In the second case, the project comprises the widening and strengthening of approximately 45 km of NH-727B from km 61.500 near Nawalpur to km 106.495 near Sikanderpur, to two -lane with paved shoulder/ four-lane with paved shoulder configuration under the engineering procurement and construction (EPC) mode in Uttar Pradesh. The project was sanctioned for Rs 2,061 crore, and EPC work was awarded to the joint venture of VRC Constructions (India) Pvt Ltd and R & C Infra Engineers Pvt Ltd at a contract price of Rs 613 crore. Technocrats Advisory Services Pvt Ltd had been appointed as the authority engineer for the project. "An incident occurred on March 25, 2026, at about 1015 hours during the execution of reinforcement works for the viaduct portion of the major bridge over River Ghaghra at Chainage km 77+220. "During the lifting and erection of the reinforcement cage for the viaduct pier, a portion of the cage collapsed and fell on workers present at the site, resulting in two fatalities and grievous injury to one person," the order document said.

item.title: Cockroach protests pose fresh challenge for Modi govt amid voter roll row
item.description: Opposition demands for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over voter-roll revisions have put the government under pressure, as arrests and security restrictions risk fuelling wider protests ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / India News / Cockroach protests pose fresh challenge for Modi govt amid voter roll row

Cockroach protests pose fresh challenge for Modi govt amid voter roll row Opposition demands for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over voter-roll revisions have put the government under pressure, as arrests and security restrictions risk fuelling wider protests

Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party take part in a protest march in New Delhi | Image: Bloomberg

Bloomberg 7 min read Last Updated : Oct 18 2026 | 3:12 PM IST

Listen to This Article

By Shruti Srivastava and Sudhi Ranjan Sen   Back in July, the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s education minister swiftly ended India’s first major round of student “Cockroach” protests just as they were gaining momentum. This time, he has no easy way out.    Modi’s rivals are now demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, alleging that he has failed to address criticism that a once-in-20-year update of India’s electoral rolls is unjustly purging millions of voters at the expense of the opposition. While there’s little hard evidence of bias, the furor was stoked by an Indian Express report last month that found Kumar ignored objections to the process raised by his two fellow commissioners.

Even if Modi wanted to get rid of Kumar, who has more than two years left on his term, the process would take time and political capital. The Election Commission of India is an independent body, and removing its head would require an investigation to prove “misbehavior” as well as approval by both houses of parliament in the same session with at least two-thirds of members present.    But Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party has repeatedly backed the Election Commission and the revision of electoral rolls, which is intended to remove dead, duplicate and ineligible voters in the world’s largest democracy. A sudden U-turn to get rid of Kumar or halt the revision process would not only hand a victory to Modi’s opponents, but also call into question recent election wins for his party, which retains a dominant grip on parliament.

Also Read

Mass demonstrations in France spiral into worst violence in decades

Rioters loot stores, set fires in Italy during cost-of-living protest

CJP's Abhijeet Dipke granted conditional bail, asked to sign peace bond

Delhi Police files multiple FIRs over CJP's 'Lehra Do Tiranga' protest

Protests against CEC, SIR will continue despite interventions: Prakash Raj

“Either you figure out a way of letting him step aside, or you ensure that the protests are delegitimized,” said Neelanjan Sircar, a political scientist at Ahmedabad University who specializes in Indian elections and voter behavior. “The government is very much on the back foot. But when you’re a dominant party with this kind of control, it can take a very long time for the slide to show.”   The dynamics leave Modi little choice but to deploy repressive measures to snuff out the protests to avoid a repeat of July, when police bloodied thousands of students in street clashes near parliament in New Delhi. His government this time has opted for mass detentions, arrests of the Cockroach Janta Party’s leaders and a partial lockdown of the capital.

Central Delhi has effectively been turned into a fortress for over a week, with heavy security and restrictions on public assembly. Roads around one of the capital’s busiest commercial districts reopened on the weekend, though barricades remained in place and thousands of security personnel are deployed across the city.    The government has also stepped up its rhetoric against the protesters, painting them as a small minority seeking to overthrow the will of voters who have helped Modi’s BJP dominate Indian politics since 2014. Unlike the earlier protests related to exams, which resonated across the political spectrum and the wider public, the latest demonstrations are more led by the opposition INDIA alliance, which has struggled in recent elections.

“Attempts are being made to use the nation’s youth as pawns in a politics of chaos — some seek a regime change,” Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said in a national address on Friday. “Their struggle is not for electoral reform,” he added, accusing protesters of seeking to “dismantle democratic institutions and set the country ablaze.”   The bet from Modi now is that the heavy security presence and arrests will help keep people off the streets long enough for the current wave of protests to fizzle out. The traffic gridlock and other inconveniences from the heightened restrictions also may increase public anger toward the protesters, particularly as the extent of disapproval over alleged election malpractices is still unclear.

Home Minister Amit Shah has also used the issue to appeal to the BJP’s base of Hindu nationalists, who want to eliminate special provisions for religious minorities including Muslims. He has accused opponents of the voter-roll revision of supporting illegal immigration, signaling that the bulk of those removed from the list are foreigners from Muslim communities in neighboring countries such as Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, according to Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, a New Delhi-based author and Modi biographer.    “I expect more draconian measures, including the use of laws against protesters and the opposition, over the next two years,” Mukhopadhyay said. “I also see a greater risk of communal tensions across the country, with minor confrontations potentially escalating into major incidents.”

At the same time, the crackdown risks backfiring into a fresh rallying cry for young people, opposition parties and civil society groups. The spotlight again is quickly turning from a single issue to Modi’s government more broadly, at a time when inflation is rising and fresh graduates are struggling to find jobs as companies seek to deploy artificial intelligence to boost productivity. The rupee is hovering near record lows and foreign investors continue to sell Indian stocks.    While Kumar hasn’t explicitly referenced the calls to resign, the Election Commission has shown more responsiveness to public criticism of late.    Last month, it agreed to publish minutes of meetings, eased some voter-verification requirements, extended deadlines for voters to challenge their exclusions in Delhi and Maharashtra, and established a panel to review its voter-registration software. The poll body also said officials would collect documents from voters with unmatched or inconsistent records, while those excluded in earlier revisions could seek reinstatement.

Modi’s best pathway to a swift resolution may come from another independent institution: The Supreme Court.    India’s top court, which previously allowed the voter-roll revision to continue, asked the poll body on Oct. 15 to respond to allegations that large numbers of eligible voters were removed from the lists. If judges order changes to the process, the government could point to the ruling rather than street pressure as the reason for a shift.   “To me, the only viable option that is available now is for judiciary to step in and work toward negotiated solution which restores the credibility of the process,” said Mujibur Rehman, a Jamia Millia Islamia political scientist and author who has written extensively on Indian politics and political institutions.

Even if that happens, the latest episode shows an even bigger problem: The Cockroach Janta Party has some staying power and isn’t going away easily. The pressure group, which has so far stayed out of electoral politics, has helped mobilize a street force that has given momentum to the INDIA opposition bloc in parliament and put Modi on the defensive.   The next major tests at the polls is slated for early next year in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, which is crucial to any opposition hopes to unseat Modi’s government in the next national vote scheduled for 2029. So far Modi’s coalition government has shown no sign of breaking apart to potentially trigger an early election.

The government is increasingly “anxious” about the cockroach movement, but it’s unclear if opposition parties will be able to convert the anger on the streets into votes at the ballot box, said Milan Vaishnav, director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace and an expert on Indian electoral politics.   “The real challenge is whether the INDIA alliance can translate this in electoral terms,” he said. “They are quite capable of snatching defeat from the jaws of victory."
